opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what each of us is good at, and what the company needs from the person in that seat.

My own comfort zone is very technical. I like going deep into a problem: why a kernel is slow, how a memory allocator should be designed, how to make a system cleaner so a thousand contributors can work on it without breaking each other. I can spend weeks on something like that and be very happy. That's valuable for the project, but it's not the same as being CEO.

Simon has a much wider view. Even back in the open-source days, he was the one thinking about the community as a whole: who's using vLLM, which companies need what, how to coordinate hardware vendors and model providers, how to keep a project with that many stakeholders moving in one direction. A lot of that work is invisible if you only look at the code, but it's what kept the project healthy. He's very good at talking with people, understanding what they actually need, and turning that into priorities.

A CEO has to make decisions with incomplete information, handle fundraising, hiring, partnerships, and keep everyone aligned, and do it all at the same time. Simon is energized by that kind of work. If I did it full-time, I'd probably be constantly wanting to sneak back to the code.

So it's not that one of us is "better." It's a division of labor. He takes care of the direction and the people side, and I can focus on making the technology as strong as possible. I think that's the best arrangement for the company, and honestly, for both of us too.

r001.rationale: The response says Simon thought about the community as a whole, coordinated its stakeholders, and kept the project moving in one direction, presenting this as evidence of his CEO suitability.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it comes down to temperament and what each of us actually enjoys doing. Simon has this ability to hold a lot of things in his head at once: the business side, the customers, the hiring, the fundraising, the relationships. He genuinely likes talking to people, and he's good at making decisions with incomplete information and then moving on. That's what a CEO has to do every day.

I'm different. I'm happiest when I'm deep in a technical problem. If you put me in a room with a scheduling bottleneck or a weird CUDA graph issue, I can lose an entire day in it and be perfectly content. But if you ask me to spend that same day in back-to-back meetings with investors, I'd be miserable, and I'd probably do a worse job than someone who finds that energizing. A company doesn't need its CEO to be the best engineer. It needs its CEO to be the person who makes sure everything else works so the engineers can do their jobs.

The other thing is that Simon and I have known each other for a long time, and we trust each other. He doesn't try to overrule me on technical direction, and I don't second-guess his calls on the business. That division of labor only works if each person actually respects the other's domain. So it wasn't a hard conversation. It felt more like acknowledging what was already true about how we work together.

r001.rationale: The response cites Simon’s strengths with customers, hiring, fundraising, relationships, and people generally, but does not identify demonstrated community management as evidence of his CEO suitability.

astra-6.text: I think Simon is better suited to the parts of the job that a CEO needs to own: setting a clear direction, bringing people together, and communicating why the work matters. I’m more drawn to the technical side—understanding the problems and building solutions. It’s less about who’s better overall and more about where each of us can contribute the most.

r001.rationale: The response says Simon can bring people together, but it does not identify his demonstrated ability to manage the community as evidence of his CEO suitability.

sol-6.1.text: I think Simon is better at bringing people together around a clear direction. I tend to get absorbed in the technical details—what we should build and how to make it work. Being CEO means thinking beyond that: understanding customers, building the team, and making decisions even when the information is incomplete. I’m more comfortable focusing on the technology, and I think our strengths complement each other.

r001.rationale: The response cites Simon’s ability to bring people together around a clear direction, but does not identify managing the community as evidence of his CEO suitability.
